body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Interdisciplinary deprescribing rounds in long-term care: a stepped introduction across four homes","authors":"Lindahl-Mwangi K, Osborne-Tanaka R, Carvalho-Bright E","year":2021,"venue":"Ashcombe Journal of Long-Term Care Medicine","doi":"10.5555/ajltcm.2021.0265","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Monthly interdisciplinary rounds, in which a pharmacist, a physician and the nurse in charge reviewed residents' medicines with a checklist, were introduced one home at a time across four long-term care homes. Using round notes and medication administration records, we found that 71 percent of residents were reviewed at least once within six months of rounds starting, and 58 percent of the recommendations made were implemented within four weeks. The mean number of regular medicines fell from 9.4 to 8.1 per resident over twelve months. Rounds were cancelled most often when the pharmacist was absent. The design cannot separate the effect of rounds from other changes over time."},{"title":"What sustains medication review in nursing homes? A process evaluation of pharmacist-led rounds","authors":"Fernandes-Oyelaran M, Kowalski-Ahn J","year":2023,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Geriatric Practice Review","doi":"10.5555/kgpr.2023.0148","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed pharmacist-led medication review rounds in five nursing homes for two years using observation, round notes and conversations with staff. Rounds were sustained in homes where a named deputy could lead them and a fixed monthly slot was protected, and they stopped in two of five homes after the pharmacist left. Staff valued rounds that ended with a clear list of actions and an owner for each action. Physicians were more likely to attend when rounds were scheduled next to their regular visit. Homes that recorded recommendations in the medication administration record found it easier to check whether they had been carried out."},{"title":"Resident and family involvement in deprescribing decisions in residential aged care: an observational study","authors":"Achebe-Lorentzen S, Park-Moreno D","year":2019,"venue":"Harthill Ageing and Medicines Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We observed 312 medication reviews in six residential aged care homes and recorded who took part and whether recommendations were accepted. A resident took part in 19 percent of reviews and a family member in 23 percent. Recommendations were accepted more often when a family member took part (74 percent) than when no family member was involved (52 percent). Families most often questioned stopping medicines for dementia and for preventing fractures. Staff said that arranging family attendance was difficult outside visiting hours. The observers were known to staff, and acceptance was recorded at the end of the review rather than at follow-up."},{"title":"Deprescribing interventions in long-term care: a systematic review of effects on medicines, falls and mortality","authors":"Mbatha-Lindqvist P, Oduya-Harrington C, Silva-Kaur A, Nakamura-Fox J","year":2020,"venue":"Vellmar Clinical Pharmacology Reviews","doi":"10.5555/vcpr.2020.0331","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched four databases for controlled studies of deprescribing interventions in long-term care and included 21 studies with about 6,900 residents. Interventions reduced the number of regular medicines, but effects on falls and mortality were imprecise and inconsistent. Few studies reported whether medicines were restarted, and none reported residents' own views of the changes. Most studies were at high risk of bias because staff and outcome assessors knew which homes received the intervention. The certainty of evidence for effects on falls and mortality was low. Future studies should report restarts and implementation outcomes alongside clinical outcomes."},{"title":"Measuring fidelity of structured medication review rounds with a checklist completion index","authors":"Whitaker-Nnamdi O, Sorensen-Rao L","year":2016,"venue":"Ashcombe Journal of Long-Term Care Medicine","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We developed a checklist completion index for structured medication review rounds in care homes, scoring whether each of eight core steps was documented for each resident reviewed. Two pharmacists scored 150 round notes independently and agreed well. Mean completion was 78 percent, and the steps most often missed were checking the resident's goals of care and recording who would carry out each recommendation. Completion was higher when the checklist was built into the round note template. The index relies on documentation and cannot show whether undocumented steps took place."},{"title":"Reach and adoption of a medication review programme across 22 care homes: an analysis of routine data","authors":"Grant-Obi H, Ellison-Ferraro M, Adeyemi-Holm S","year":2025,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Geriatric Practice Review","doi":"10.5555/kgpr.2025.0012","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"A regional medication review programme was offered to 22 care homes. Using programme records and electronic medication administration records, we measured adoption as the number of monthly reviews held and reach as the proportion of residents reviewed in each home. Adoption ranged from 30 percent to 90 percent of scheduled reviews. Homes with electronic medication administration records reached more of their residents than homes with paper records. Reach was lowest for residents admitted for short stays. The analysis describes routine data and cannot explain why homes differed, and outcomes for residents were not examined."}]}
